nodes.label: Najd and the Saudi–Wahhabi state
nodes.full: The reviving Al Saud emirate in the Arabian interior under Ibn Saud — its Ikhwan raiders press the Kuwait frontier, its oil-company-backed claim reaches for the Buraimi oasis, and its very existence is what makes hard desert borders necessary.
nodes.src: background — Dickson, 'Kuwait and her Neighbours' (1956); Kelly, 'Eastern Arabian Frontiers' (1964)

nodes.label: The world pearl market and Japanese cultured pearls
nodes.full: The Bombay and Paris dealers whose demand drove the pearling boom — and the cultured pearls Mikimoto brought to market in the 1920s, which together with the Depression destroyed the natural pearl's value and the Gulf economy with it.
nodes.src: background — Carter, 'Sea of Pearls' (2012)

nodes.label: The Political Resident and the treaty system
nodes.full: From 1820 the Government of India managed the Gulf's Arab coast through a Political Resident and a network of Political Agents. Britain controlled the shaykhdoms' foreign relations, defence and — increasingly — their internal succession, without formally annexing an inch.
nodes.src: Onley, 'The Arabian Frontier of the British Raj' (2007); the Residency moved from Bushire to Bahrain in 1946.

nodes.label: Zayed bin Khalifa — 'Zayed the First' of Abu Dhabi
nodes.full: Zayed bin Khalifa held Abu Dhabi for 54 years, making it the strongest of the Trucial shaykhdoms through control of the Liwa date gardens, the pearl banks and the Buraimi oasis. His long reign is the benchmark of Al Nahyan authority.
nodes.src: Heard-Bey, 'From Trucial States to United Arab Emirates' (1982); Lorimer, 'Gazetteer of the Persian Gulf' (1908–15).

nodes.label: The Al Maktoum secession and Dubai's free port
nodes.full: In 1833 the Al Bu Falasah section of the Bani Yas broke away from Abu Dhabi under Maktoum bin Butti and settled Dubai Creek. In 1894 Shaikh Maktoum bin Hasher abolished commercial duties — the decision that made Dubai the coast's great trading port.
nodes.src: Heard-Bey (1982); the 1833 secession and the 1894 free-trade decree that drew merchants from Persian Lingeh.

nodes.label: Shakhbut deposed; Zayed bin Sultan accedes in Abu Dhabi
nodes.full: Shaikh Shakhbut, distrustful of the new oil money and slow to spend it, was replaced by his brother Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan in a bloodless family move backed by Britain. Zayed's development drive and diplomacy made him the architect of the federation five years later.
nodes.src: the 1966 accession of Zayed bin Sultan; Heard-Bey (1982); Zayed had been Ruler's Representative in Al Ain since 1946.

nodes.label: Britain deposes the ruler of Bahrain
nodes.full: When Shaikh Muhammad bin Khalifa broke the maritime peace by attacking Qatar, the Royal Navy bombarded, deposed and exiled him, installing his brother Isa. It was the clearest demonstration that under the treaties Britain, not the ruling family, had the last word on the throne.
nodes.src: the 1868 events; the resulting recognition of the Al Thani in Qatar; Lorimer (1908–15); Onley (2007).

nodes.label: The Al Thani recognised in Qatar; the Ottoman interlude
nodes.full: Britain's 1868 dealings with Muhammad bin Thani effectively founded Qatar as an entity separate from Bahrain. An Ottoman garrison held Doha from 1871 to 1915; the 1916 treaty then brought Qatar fully into the British Trucial system under Shaikh Abdullah bin Jassim.
nodes.src: Rahman, 'The Emergence of Qatar' (2005); the 1868 agreement and the 1916 treaty.

nodes.label: Mubarak the Great and the 1899 Kuwait agreement
nodes.full: Mubarak Al Sabah seized power by killing his brothers, then — fearing Ottoman absorption and a German railway terminus on his bay — signed a secret agreement in 1899 placing Kuwait's foreign relations in British hands. It set Kuwait's course for the next 60 years.
nodes.src: Anscombe, 'The Ottoman Gulf' (1997); the secret Anglo-Kuwaiti Agreement of 1899.

nodes.label: The five smaller shaykhdoms recognised
nodes.full: Alongside Abu Dhabi and Dubai, Britain recognised Sharjah and Ajman and Umm al-Quwain from the start, Ras al-Khaimah as separate from Sharjah in 1921, and Fujairah only in 1952 — fixing the seven rulers who would later federate.
nodes.src: Heard-Bey (1982); the sequence of British recognition of the Trucial rulers.

nodes.label: The Trucial States Council
nodes.full: Britain brought the seven rulers together in a consultative council under the chairmanship of the Political Agent — the first standing institution the Trucial Coast had ever had, and the seed of the federal structure adopted in 1971.
nodes.src: the Trucial States Council (1952); the Trucial States Development Office (1965); Heard-Bey (1982).

nodes.label: The destruction of Ras al-Khaimah and the 1820 treaty
nodes.full: An East India Company expedition captured and demolished the Qawasim capital, then the shaykhs of the coast signed the General Maritime Treaty renouncing 'plunder and piracy' by sea. British sea power now underwrote the treaty order.
nodes.src: the 1819 campaign and the 1820 General Maritime Treaty (Kelly, 'Britain and the Persian Gulf 1795–1880', 1968).

nodes.label: The Qatar–Bahrain war and British intervention
nodes.full: A Bahraini and Abu Dhabi attack devastated Doha and Wakra; the Qataris retaliated at sea. Britain treated the whole affair as a breach of the maritime truce, punishing Bahrain and dealing separately with Qatar — the moment Qatar's separate identity was recognised.
nodes.src: Rahman, 'The Emergence of Qatar' (2005); the 1868 settlement.

nodes.label: The Battle of Al Wajbah
nodes.full: Shaikh Jassim bin Muhammad Al Thani's fighters ambushed and defeated an Ottoman punitive column sent from Doha. The victory, though it did not end the Ottoman garrison, is remembered as the founding assertion of Qatari self-rule.
nodes.src: the Battle of Al Wajbah, March 1893; Qatari national tradition; Rahman (2005).

nodes.label: The Battle of Jahra
nodes.full: Kuwaiti forces held the Red Fort at Jahra against a raid by Ibn Saud's Ikhwan, and the town wall was hurriedly built. The clash marked the violent birth of the Kuwait–Najd frontier, fixed two years later at Uqair.
nodes.src: the Battle of Jahra, October 1920; the Ikhwan raids; Dickson, 'Kuwait and her Neighbours' (1956).

nodes.label: The Buraimi dispute
nodes.full: Saudi Arabia, encouraged by its oil company, claimed the Buraimi oasis and occupied one of its villages in 1952. After arbitration collapsed, the Trucial Oman Scouts and Abu Dhabi and Omani forces evicted the Saudi party in 1955 — but the border stayed unsettled for decades.
nodes.src: Kelly, 'Eastern Arabian Frontiers' (1964); the 1952 occupation of Hamasa and the 1955 expulsion.

nodes.label: Iran seizes the Tunbs and Abu Musa
nodes.full: Two days before the British protectorate ended, Iranian forces landed on Greater and Lesser Tunb (Ras al-Khaimah) and Abu Musa (Sharjah, under a coerced sharing agreement). The islands remain under Iranian control and a live UAE claim.
nodes.src: the 30 November 1971 landings; the Sharjah–Iran Memorandum of Understanding on Abu Musa; Schofield, 'Territorial Foundations of the Gulf States' (1994).

nodes.label: From General Treaty to Perpetual Truce to Exclusive Agreement
nodes.full: The 1820 General Maritime Treaty banned war by sea; the 1835 truce, renewed until made perpetual in 1853, ended it for good — hence 'Trucial'; the 1892 Exclusive Agreements barred the rulers from ceding territory to, or dealing with, any power but Britain. The protectorate was built in three treaty steps.
nodes.src: texts in Aitchison, 'A Collection of Treaties, Engagements and Sanads'; Kelly (1968); Onley (2007).

nodes.label: The Kuwait and Qatar treaties
nodes.full: The secret 1899 Anglo-Kuwaiti Agreement and the 1916 Anglo-Qatari treaty extended the same bargain — British protection and a subsidy in exchange for an exclusive relationship — to the two Gulf shaykhdoms outside the original Trucial group.
nodes.src: the 1899 and 1916 agreements; Anscombe, 'The Ottoman Gulf' (1997); Rahman (2005).

nodes.label: The anti-slave-trade engagements and manumission at the Agencies
nodes.full: Successive treaties bound the rulers to suppress the maritime slave trade, and an enslaved person who reached a British Agency could claim a manumission certificate. Enforcement was patchy and slavery itself persisted on the coast into the 1950s and 60s.
nodes.src: the 1847, 1856 and 1873 slave-trade engagements; Suzuki, 'Slave Trade Profiteers in the Western Indian Ocean' (2017); manumission at the Bahrain and Sharjah Agencies.

nodes.label: Belgrave's Bahrain — courts, land registry and the pearling reform
nodes.full: Charles Belgrave, the ruler's British Adviser for 31 years, built Bahrain a modern administration — law courts, a land register, a police force, state schools — and in 1932 tried to reform the pearl-diving debt system just as the industry collapsed.
nodes.src: Belgrave, 'Personal Column' (1960); the 1932 'Reform of the Pearl Diving Industry'; the diver unrest of 1932 and 1938.

nodes.label: The Uqair Protocol draws the borders
nodes.full: At a conference at Uqair, the British agent Percy Cox drew the boundaries between Kuwait, Najd and Iraq on a map, creating two 'neutral zones' where the lines could not be agreed. It was the first hard border in a region that had known only tribal ranges.
nodes.src: the Uqair Protocol, December 1922; Dickson, 'Kuwait and her Neighbours' (1956); Finnie, 'Shifting Lines in the Sand' (1992).

nodes.label: The Arabian Mission and the first modern hospitals
nodes.full: The Reformed Church's Arabian Mission opened the Gulf's first modern hospitals and schools. Its doctors — including women like Sarah Hosmon and Eleanor Calverley — treated tens of thousands and won a tolerated place, while making almost no converts.
nodes.src: Mason & Barny, 'History of the Arabian Mission' (1926); the Mason Memorial Hospital, Bahrain (1903).

nodes.label: The Shia communities of the treaty coast
nodes.full: Shia communities — the settled Baharna of Bahrain, the Persian 'Ajam' of the Trucial ports, the Hasawiyya — kept their own courts, mosques and mourning houses (ma'tams) under Sunni rulers and a British paramountcy that mostly left religious affairs alone.
nodes.src: Fuccaro, 'Histories of City and State in the Persian Gulf: Manama since 1800' (2009); the ma'tam institution.

nodes.label: Reformist Islam reaches the coast
nodes.full: Through returning students, imported teachers and print, reformist and Salafi ideas — and later the Muslim Brotherhood, carried by Egyptian teachers in the 1950s — spread among the coast's small educated class, feeding both religious revival and anti-colonial politics.
nodes.src: Freer, 'Rentier Islamism' (2018) on the Brotherhood in the Gulf; the role of Egyptian and Palestinian teachers in the 1950s.

nodes.label: The Omani Imamate revived in the interior
nodes.full: Beyond the Trucial Coast, the Ibadi tribes of interior Oman re-established an elected Imamate under the 1920 Treaty of Seeb, autonomous from the British-backed Sultan in Muscat, until the Sultan's forces — with British air support — crushed it in the 1950s.
nodes.src: the 1920 Treaty of Seeb; the Jebel Akhdar War (1954–59); Peterson, 'Oman's Insurgencies' (2007).

nodes.label: The coral-and-gypsum wind-tower house
nodes.full: The pearling merchants built courtyard houses of coral stone and gypsum plaster, topped by wind-towers (barjeel) that funnelled the breeze down into the rooms. Muharraq and the Dubai Creekside quarter of Bastakiya preserve the finest surviving examples.
nodes.src: Bastakiya / Al Fahidi historical district, Dubai; the Bahrain Pearling Path (Muharraq), UNESCO World Heritage (2012); Coles & Jackson, 'Windtower' (2007).

nodes.label: Sharjah's airfield fort and the rest-house
nodes.full: When Imperial Airways made Sharjah a night-stop on the Britain–India route, a small fortified rest-house was built beside the airstrip, guarded by the ruler's men. It is a monument to the moment the Trucial Coast joined the age of air travel — and to the airfield rent that kept Sharjah solvent.
nodes.src: the Sharjah Al Mahatta rest-house (now the Al Mahatta Museum); the 1932 Imperial Airways agreement.

nodes.label: The Political Agency archive and early Gulf photography
nodes.full: British officers, and travellers like Wilfred Thesiger who crossed the Empty Quarter from the Trucial Coast in 1946–50, left thousands of photographs and reports — the visual and documentary record of a society on the eve of oil.
nodes.src: the India Office Records (British Library); Thesiger's photographs (Pitt Rivers Museum, Oxford); 'Arabian Sands' (1959).

nodes.label: Nabati poetry and the ruler-poets
nodes.full: The vernacular Nabati verse of the Gulf — recited at the majlis, exchanged between rulers, sung by the pearling crews — carried political argument, praise, satire and lament. Several shaykhs were accomplished poets in the form.
nodes.src: Sowayan, 'Nabati Poetry: The Oral Poetry of Arabia' (1985); the Gulf Nabati tradition.

nodes.label: Lorimer's Gazetteer of the Persian Gulf
nodes.full: J. G. Lorimer's two-volume 'Gazetteer' — a historical narrative and a district-by-district geography of every tribe, town, well and pearl-boat — was compiled as a secret handbook for British officers. It is the single richest source for the Gulf of the 19th century.
nodes.src: J. G. Lorimer, 'Gazetteer of the Persian Gulf, Oman and Central Arabia' (Historical vol. 1915; Geographical vol. 1908).

nodes.label: The majlis movements of 1938
nodes.full: In the depths of the post-pearl depression, reform movements in Kuwait, Dubai and Bahrain demanded elected legislative councils, budget transparency and an end to arbitrary rule. All three were suppressed within months — but they set the template for Gulf constitutional politics.
nodes.src: Crystal, 'Oil and Politics in the Gulf' (1990); al-Nakib, 'Kuwait Transformed' (2016); the Dubai Reform Movement of 1938.

nodes.label: Modern schooling begins
nodes.full: Kuwait's merchant-funded al-Mubarakiyya school (1911) began modern education in the Gulf; Bahrain followed in 1919, and the Trucial Coast's first state schools opened in the 1950s, many paid for by Kuwait. Literacy and a salaried professional class grew from these beginnings.
nodes.src: al-Nakib, 'Kuwait Transformed' (2016); Davidson, 'The United Arab Emirates: A Study in Survival' (2005) on Trucial education.

nodes.label: The press and the Gulf nahda
nodes.full: Kuwait's magazine 'al-Kuwait' (1928), Bahrain's newspapers and the literary clubs of both towns carried a small cultural awakening — poetry, translation, debate about reform and Arab identity — that fed directly into the politics of the 1950s.
nodes.src: the Gulf press history (al-Rasheed and others); 'al-Kuwait' magazine (1928), founded by Abd al-Aziz al-Rushaid.

nodes.label: The pearling golden age
nodes.full: Rising European and Indian demand drove the Gulf pearl trade to its peak: thousands of boats, tens of thousands of men at sea each summer, and merchant fortunes made in the Bombay and Paris markets. Pearls were up to nine-tenths of the Trucial economy.
nodes.src: Carter, 'Sea of Pearls' (2012); Lorimer's pearling statistics; Lienhardt, 'Shaikhdoms of Eastern Arabia' (2001).

nodes.label: The pearl crash
nodes.full: The Great Depression cut demand just as cheap Japanese cultured pearls destroyed the natural pearl's premium. The Gulf market collapsed within a few years, plunging the pearling towns into a decade of poverty, hunger and emigration — the 'years of hunger'.
nodes.src: Carter, 'Sea of Pearls' (2012); the impact of Mikimoto cultured pearls and the 1929 crash; Heard-Bey (1982).

nodes.label: Dubai the entrepôt
nodes.full: Free of duties, Dubai drew the Persian merchants of Lingeh from about 1900 and became the coast's re-export hub. Through the depression and after, its trade — including the 1950s–60s gold runs to India — kept the town alive while its neighbours starved.
nodes.src: Davidson, 'Dubai: The Vulnerability of Success' (2008); the Lingeh merchant migration; the gold trade to the Indian subcontinent.

nodes.label: Oil comes ashore
nodes.full: Bahrain struck oil in 1932; Kuwait and Qatar exported after the war; Abu Dhabi's first cargo left in 1962 and Dubai's in 1969. Within a decade oil royalties turned the poorest shaykhdoms on Earth into states with the means to build everything at once.
nodes.src: the concession and discovery dates; Abu Dhabi's Umm Shaif (offshore, 1958) and Bab (onshore, 1960); Dubai's Fateh field (1966).

nodes.label: Airfield rent and the staging posts
nodes.full: The rent Imperial Airways paid to land at Sharjah, and the fees from Bahrain and the Dubai marine base, were among the few cash incomes of the depression years — for Sharjah, the airfield was for a time the ruler's largest single revenue.
nodes.src: the 1932 Sharjah air agreement; Stanley-Price, 'Imperial Outpost in the Gulf: The Airfield at Sharjah' (2012).

nodes.label: From the rupee to the riyal and the dirham
nodes.full: The Gulf used the Indian rupee, then a special 'Gulf rupee' from 1959. India's 1966 devaluation forced the shaykhdoms to issue their own money — the Bahrain dinar, the Qatar and Dubai riyal, and finally the UAE dirham — a first step toward economic sovereignty.
nodes.src: the Gulf rupee (1959–66) and its replacement; Krozewski and others on Gulf decolonisation finance.

nodes.label: The Indo-European telegraph down the Gulf
nodes.full: The line laid to carry messages between London and British India ran down the Gulf, with a cable along its bed. It was the first modern communications infrastructure the region had, and it tied the Gulf's tempo to imperial news.
nodes.src: the Indo-European Telegraph Department; the 1864 Gulf section (Bushire–Fao–Karachi).

nodes.label: Kuwait pioneers large-scale desalination
nodes.full: With almost no groundwater and a growing oil town, Kuwait built one of the world's first large multi-stage flash distillation plants, turning seawater into drinking water at industrial scale. Every Gulf city's growth would later depend on the technology Kuwait proved.
nodes.src: Kuwait's early MSF desalination (from 1953); the Gulf as the cradle of large-scale seawater distillation.

nodes.label: Dredging Dubai Creek
nodes.full: Shaikh Rashid borrowed from Kuwait and raised a customs-backed bond to dredge the silting Creek so ocean vessels could enter. The project — completed just as Dubai's own oil was found — is the origin of Dubai's strategy of building infrastructure ahead of demand.
nodes.src: the 1959–63 Creek dredging; the Halcrow scheme; Davidson, 'Dubai: The Vulnerability of Success' (2008).

nodes.label: Offshore oil and the Das Island terminal
nodes.full: Abu Dhabi's largest oil lay under the seabed. Fixed platforms, subsea pipelines and a tank farm and export jetty built on tiny Das Island brought it ashore — a heavy-engineering complex assembled on a sandbar 160 km offshore.
nodes.src: the development of Umm Shaif (1958) and Zakum; the Das Island terminal (ADMA).

nodes.label: The Gulf run from India
nodes.full: Until 1947 the Gulf was managed by the Government of India, not the Foreign Office — its currency the rupee, its agents often Persian or Indian merchants, its garrisons Indian troops. Economically and administratively the Gulf was a western outwork of the Raj.
nodes.src: Onley, 'The Arabian Frontier of the British Raj' (2007); the transfer of Gulf responsibility to the Foreign Office in 1947.

nodes.label: The Lingeh merchants and the Ajam of the coast
nodes.full: When Persia imposed customs and control on its own Gulf ports, Sunni and Shia merchant families from Lingeh and Bastak crossed to the duty-free Arab side, above all to Dubai. Their capital and networks built the modern Creek trade.
nodes.src: the migration from Lingeh after c.1900; Fuccaro (2009); Davidson (2008) on the Bastakiya community.

nodes.label: The oil-era labour turn
nodes.full: In the 1930s and 40s Trucial Coast men left to work the Bahrain and Saudi oilfields; from the 1960s the flow reversed as Abu Dhabi and Dubai drew workers from India, Pakistan, Iran and the wider Arab world. The Gulf's demographic transformation had begun.
nodes.src: the pre-war emigration to the oil towns; the post-1960 labour immigration (Heard-Bey 1982; Davidson 2005).

nodes.label: Arab nationalism reaches the Gulf
nodes.full: Cairo Radio, Egyptian and Palestinian teachers, and returning students carried Nasserist and Ba'thist ideas into the Gulf. Strikes and demonstrations — Bahrain 1954–56, the 1965 Bahrain intifada — pressed the rulers and Britain alike.
nodes.src: the Bahrain National Union movement (1954–56); Cairo Radio's Gulf reach; Smith, 'Britain's Revival and Fall in the Gulf' (2004).

nodes.label: The federation of nine that failed
nodes.full: After Britain's withdrawal announcement, Zayed of Abu Dhabi and Rashid of Dubai agreed to unite, and invited the other five Trucial states, Bahrain and Qatar to join. Bahrain and Qatar chose separate independence; the six — then seven — formed the UAE.
nodes.src: the February 1968 Zayed–Rashid meeting; the Federation of Arab Emirates talks (1968–71); Bahrain and Qatar to independence, August–September 1971.

nodes.label: Keeping the rivals out
nodes.full: British Gulf policy was defensive: exclude Russia, then the Ottomans, then Germany (whose Baghdad Railway aimed at a Kuwait terminus) from a sea that was the western approach to India. The treaties with the shaykhs were the instruments of that exclusion.
nodes.src: Busch, 'Britain and the Persian Gulf 1894–1914' (1967); the Baghdad Railway question.

nodes.label: Persian oil and the Royal Navy's fuel
nodes.full: Oil struck in Persia in 1908, and the Royal Navy's switch from coal to oil under Churchill in 1912, made the Gulf's oil potential a first-order British strategic interest — years before a barrel was found on the Arab side.
nodes.src: the Anglo-Persian Oil Company (1909); the 1913–14 British government stake; Yergin, 'The Prize' (1991).

nodes.label: The World Wars and the Gulf
nodes.full: The Mesopotamia campaign of 1914–18 was launched from Basra and ended Ottoman Qatar; in 1941–45 the Gulf was the 'Persian Corridor' funnelling Allied supplies to the Soviet Union, and the first American airbase opened at Dhahran in 1945.
nodes.src: the WWI Mesopotamia campaign; the Persian Corridor (Motter, 'The Persian Corridor and Aid to Russia', 1952).

nodes.label: Britain announces the retreat from East of Suez
nodes.full: A sterling crisis pushed the Labour government to announce that Britain would give up all its military commitments east of Suez, including the Gulf, by the end of 1971. The shaykhdoms had three years to build states of their own.
nodes.src: the January 1968 defence review; Smith, 'Britain's Revival and Fall in the Gulf' (2004).

nodes.label: Independence week
nodes.full: Bahrain declared independence on 15 August 1971, Qatar on 3 September, and the United Arab Emirates was proclaimed on 2 December, with Ras al-Khaimah joining in February 1972. A century and a half of British paramountcy ended in four months.
nodes.src: the 1971 independence dates; the UAE's formation on 2 December 1971.

nodes.label: The years of hunger
nodes.full: With the pearl trade dead and no oil money yet, the 1930s and early 40s were years of real destitution on the Trucial Coast — families splitting up, men emigrating to the oilfields, and, in the worst years, deaths from hunger and disease.
nodes.src: oral histories and Agency reports of the 1930s depression; Heard-Bey (1982); Lienhardt, 'Shaikhdoms of Eastern Arabia' (2001).

nodes.label: Manumission and the long end of Gulf slavery
nodes.full: Enslaved people — most of East African origin, working as divers, servants and labourers — could seek a manumission certificate at a British Agency, and hundreds did. Slavery was only progressively abolished on the coast: Qatar in 1952, Saudi Arabia in 1962, Oman in 1970.
nodes.src: the manumission statements in the India Office Records (a major source of enslaved Africans' own testimony); Hopper, 'Slaves of One Master' (2015).

nodes.label: The mission doctors and the first women's healthcare
nodes.full: Women physicians of the Arabian Mission — Sarah Hosmon, Eleanor Calverley and others — ran the Gulf's first clinics for women, at a time when male doctors could not examine them. Their patient registers are among the earliest health records of Gulf women.
nodes.src: Calverley, 'My Arabian Days and Nights' (1958); Scudder, 'The Arabian Mission's Story' (1998).

nodes.label: The Ajam — a people of both shores
nodes.full: The Persian-origin 'Ajam' of the Trucial ports — Sunni Bastakis and Shia Lingehis alike — became merchants, builders and craftsmen central to Dubai's growth, holding an identity poised between the Arab coast where they lived and the Persian one they came from.
nodes.src: Fuccaro, 'Histories of City and State in the Persian Gulf' (2009); the Ajam communities of Dubai and Sharjah.
